Chapter 4: The Realities of the Prison System and Its Impact on Identity
The longer someone spends behind bars, the more the cracks and contradictions of the prison system start to show. What’s meant to be a place for turning lives around... often just feels like a warehouse for people society would rather forget. There are rules for everything—strict ones, too—but if you try to figure out the logic? It’s not always clear. Instead of focusing on genuine change, the main goal seems to be control and compliance. You notice the inefficiencies everywhere you look. Even basic medical care can feel out of reach, with endless waits for the simplest treatment. If you ask for help, there’s a good chance you’ll be ignored or brushed aside. The system’s a maze of paperwork, and the staff? Most are stretched thin, or just plain indifferent. And if you’re struggling with mental health, things only get tougher. There’s a heavy stigma, and hardly any resources. Sure, there are education and job training programs on paper. But in reality, they’re limited, often underfunded, and it’s tough to get a spot. A lot of people want to use their time inside to learn, to pick up skills that might help later on. But the truth is, the system seems more interested in keeping folks busy than in helping them grow. These conditions take a toll on identity. When you lose your autonomy, when you’re constantly watched, and forced to follow rules that don’t always make sense... your confidence takes a hit. People become numbers. Individuality gets chipped away, and the label of “criminal” sticks, changing not just how others see you, but how you see yourself. Still, even in this tough environment, people find ways to hold onto their dignity. Some take pride in their work—no matter how small the job. Others find purpose by helping newcomers get settled or being there for a friend when times get rough. Just keeping a sense of self, holding tight to your values and dreams, becomes an act of quiet resistance. Relationships with staff are complicated, too. There are guards who treat people fairly, who respect them. But there are also those who use their authority to belittle or intimidate. That line between enforcing the rules and abusing power? It’s razor-thin. And if you complain, chances are nothing changes. So, most folks learn to keep their heads down, avoid attention, and lean on each other for support. Getting ready for release brings its own set of worries. The world outside has moved on, and the weight of a criminal record can feel impossible to shake. People worry about finding a job, reconnecting with family, and rebuilding a life. There’s barely any support, and the risk of slipping back into old habits—or facing poverty again—is all too real. But here’s the thing—despite all these challenges, prison can also spark real growth. The long hours spent thinking about past choices, learning about resilience and empathy, and building bonds with others... they can lead to a deeper understanding of yourself and the world. The journey’s anything but easy, and the scars run deep. But even here, the door to redemption is never fully closed.
